routes.description: Establish sufficient warrant for Christianity by defending appropriate historical and relational modes of inquiry, the credibility of the Gospel portrayal of Jesus, the resurrection inference, and Christianity's account of moral meaning and human value.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative case gives adequate reason to trust the central Christian claims, especially Jesus's identity and resurrection, while showing that documentary, scientific, moral, and rival-religion objections do not defeat that warrant.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defended evidence for Jesus and the resurrection, together with Christianity's explanatory claims, to sufficient warrant for Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Justify using historical, documentary, and relational reasoning without treating scientific repeatability as the sole avenue to truth.
Establish that the Gospel sources preserve a sufficiently coherent and historically credible portrayal of Jesus.
Show that the reported death, empty tomb, appearances, and witness transformation are better explained by resurrection than by relevant alternatives.
Explain objective morality, human value, suffering, and human wrongdoing within a coherent Christian account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify criteria intended to distinguish Christian claims from incompatible religious claims rather than validating them symmetrically.
Distinguish Christianity's normative commitments from disputed interpretations, divine accommodation, and human misuse of scripture.

routes.description: Show that Christianity has not met its burden because its verification methods do not reliably distinguish truth from fiction or rival religions, its sources do not establish their supernatural claims, and its accounts of morality and human value face viable secular alternatives and textual objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proffered methods and evidence remain insufficient to establish the Gospel and resurrection claims, especially when tested against ordinary evidential standards, alternative explanations, internal disputes, and the distinction between transmission and truth.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved evidential and explanatory deficits to withholding affirmation that Christianity is true or sufficiently warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require truth-testing criteria that discriminate Christianity from incompatible religions, fiction, and unsupported supernatural explanations.
Separate textual preservation, consistency, and accurate background details from evidence that the Gospel claims correspond to reality.
Show that resurrection testimony and proposed historical facts do not justify a supernatural bodily-resurrection inference.
Test claims about divine moral grounding and equal human value against secular accounts and morally difficult biblical provisions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that identifying defects in an affirmative method does not require supplying a method that verifies supernatural claims.
Apply empirical scrutiny to asserted physical events even when those events are presented through historical or religious narratives.

sections.title: Truth-Testing Methods and Evidential Burdens
sections.rationale: This issue governs what would count as sufficient warrant, whether Christianity can be distinguished from rival claims, and whether criticism of an offered method incurs a separate positive burden.

sections.title: Gospel Preservation, Coherence, and Historical Reliability
sections.rationale: The Gospel documents are the principal route to claims about Jesus, so the distinction between textual transmission, literary and archaeological indicators, narrative coherence, and factual truth is central.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: The resurrection is presented as Christianity's decisive truth condition, making the death, burial, empty tomb, appearances, witnesses, narrative disagreements, and natural or supernatural explanations the largest issue.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Human Value, and Meaning
sections.rationale: The motion expressly concerns moral meaning and human value, requiring comparison of the proposed divine grounding with secular sources of meaning and moral regard.

sections.title: Scriptural Morality, Creation, Evil, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Claims about creation, gender, slavery, suffering, interpretation, accommodation, and free will test whether Christianity's texts and moral framework remain coherent with its account of divine goodness.

routes.description: Establish that meaningful proximity requires a chemically specified and experimentally credible account of producing, preserving, organizing, and integrating the components of first life, and that current work has not met that burden.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the unresolved requirements for molecular synthesis, stereochemistry, sequencing, assembly, and cellular organization outweigh appeals to abstract possibility, large opportunity spaces, elapsed time, or limited directional clues.

motionBridge.description: Show that current science lacks a sufficiently complete and credible chemical pathway to count as meaningfully close to explaining first life.

centralBridges.description: Specify the multiple molecular classes and integrated organizational steps that an origin account must explain.
Require probability and possibility claims to engage the cumulative chemistry of production, preservation, and assembly.
Determine whether experimental advances approach the explanatory target or whether growing knowledge of complexity makes that target more remote.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for whether long timescales preserve useful intermediates or instead amplify decomposition and side reactions.
Use unresolved features of cellular organization to clarify why possessing molecular components may not explain the transition to life.

routes.description: Establish that incomplete mechanistic understanding can coexist with limited scientific clues and a defensible agnostic position when the probability, opportunity space, recurrence, and recoverability of natural abiogenesis remain unresolved.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if current evidence supplies some burden-relevant direction while leaving neither natural emergence nor alternatives demonstrated or excluded, so present remoteness does not warrant treating the scientific search as devoid of explanatory contact.

motionBridge.description: Show that limited empirical or theoretical clues provide meaningful explanatory contact while still requiring agnosticism about a complete origin account.

centralBridges.description: Relate a finite natural-origin probability to the universe's unknown number of opportunities without claiming that either quantity is presently measurable.
Distinguish possessing limited directional clues from possessing a complete, demonstrated mechanism.
Identify observations, including demonstrably independent origins, that could materially change the assessment of natural abiogenesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Allow for conceptual breakthroughs that could change the pace of progress despite prolonged present confusion.
Consider whether an extraordinarily rare and unrepeatable origin could remain partly inaccessible to scientific reconstruction.

sections.title: Chemical Production, Preservation, and Cellular Assembly
sections.rationale: This issue defines the principal explanatory burden by asking what molecular classes, reaction sequences, stability conditions, and organizational steps must be accounted for before first life has a credible chemical pathway.

sections.title: Nonzero Probability and Cosmic Opportunity
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether finite reaction probabilities and an immense opportunity space support agnosticism or remain too abstract without accounting for the many required synthesis and assembly steps.

sections.title: Limited Clues and Distance from an Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the motion's meaningfully-close standard by distinguishing partial directional knowledge from a complete account and by asking whether the explanatory target is approaching or receding.

sections.title: Independent Origins as an Empirical Test
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether independently arisen extraterrestrial life would reveal that abiogenesis is naturally accessible, and whether recurrence alone would illuminate the underlying mechanism.

sections.title: Timescales, Breakthroughs, and Scientific Recoverability
sections.rationale: This issue brings together whether time aids or degrades prebiotic chemistry, whether progress may arrive discontinuously, and whether a singular rare event could be reconstructed by science at all.

routes.description: Establish that naturalism combined with evolution makes the reliability of human cognitive faculties low or inscrutable, that recognizing this condition defeats trust in those faculties, and that the defeater extends to the beliefs supporting naturalism and evolution themselves.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the reliability premise is supported through the separation of adaptive behavior from true content, awareness of low or inscrutable reliability is shown to generate a faculty-wide defeater, and that defeater is shown to include belief in naturalism and evolution.

motionBridge.description: Connect the reliability concern to a defeater for trusting the cognitive faculties of a believer who accepts naturalism and evolution.

centralBridges.description: Show that selection for adaptive neurology and behavior does not by itself select for true belief content.
Derive low or inscrutable overall cognitive reliability from the alleged independence of adaptive success and belief truth.
Explain why recognizing low or inscrutable reliability defeats confidence in faculty-produced beliefs, including the naturalistic evolutionary outlook.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the determination or supervenience of content from correspondence between that content and adaptive action.
Explain why the proposed reliability defeater is specific to naturalism rather than evolution alone, including the claimed theistic basis for expecting reliable faculties.

routes.description: Resist the alleged defeater by explaining how conceptual and causal relations among belief, neurology, behavior, and environment permit unguided evolution to favor truth-conducive cognition, while challenging the claimed special skeptical disadvantage of naturalism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if adaptive selection is shown capable of favoring generally true beliefs, the inference to low or inscrutable reliability is thereby blocked, or the resulting skeptical problem is shown not to establish a distinctive defeater for naturalistic believers.

motionBridge.description: Show that naturalism and evolution do not require their believers to acquire the alleged defeater for trusting their cognitive faculties.

centralBridges.description: Explain how accurate beliefs about relevant environmental conditions can systematically support fitness-enhancing behavior.
Show that causal, conceptual, and behavioral constraints prevent belief content from being freely detached from adaptive action.
Test whether the proposed skeptical structure uniquely burdens naturalism by considering an analogous undercutting problem for theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify that atheism does not entail naturalism and therefore does not define the full population reached by the argument.
Distinguish generally truth-conducive evolved cognition from any requirement that every evolved belief be true.

sections.title: Adaptive Selection and Truth-Conducive Cognition
sections.rationale: The principal clash concerns whether fitness-enhancing behavior supplies an evolutionary route to generally accurate representation or remains indifferent to belief truth.

sections.title: Mental Content, Neurology, and Behavioral Constraints
sections.rationale: The reliability premise depends on whether content can vary independently of adaptive neural output or is constrained by its causal and conceptual role in behavior.

sections.title: Probability of Reliable Cognitive Faculties
sections.rationale: The debate requires an account of how claims about individual belief truth aggregate into a judgment that evolved cognitive faculties are reliable, unreliable, or inscrutable.

sections.title: Defeater Generation and Epistemic Self-Reference
sections.rationale: Even if reliability is doubtful, the motion turns on whether awareness of that doubt defeats faculty trust and extends to the naturalistic evolutionary beliefs that produced it.

sections.title: Worldview Scope and Theistic Symmetry
sections.rationale: The scope and distinctiveness of the argument depend on how naturalism differs from atheism and whether a parallel faculty-undermining problem arises for the proposed theistic alternative.

moves.proposition: If naturalism and evolution are both true, the probability that human cognitive faculties are reliable is low.
moves.attributionBasis: Plantinga explicitly announces the beginning of his argument and labels this probability claim as its first premise.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the central probabilistic premise and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states an indispensable premise, though it does not yet supply its supporting mechanism.

routes.description: Establish robust non-naturalist normative realism by treating objective normative facts as legitimate explananda, defending normative appearances as justified starting points, and showing that realism best preserves ordinary judgment, deliberation, and language under holistic comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective normative facts remain warranted components of inquiry, challenges from intuition diversity and causal genealogy do not defeat that warrant, and rival pragmatist or attitude-based accounts fail to explain the relevant normative phenomena without comparable commitments.

motionBridge.description: Connect justified mind-independent normative facts, including moral facts, to the motion's claim that objective moral truths exist and favor realism over global normative anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Show why normative facts themselves, rather than only beliefs, behavior, or linguistic practices, are legitimate phenomena requiring explanation.
Explain why plausible normative appearances can justify inquiry without prior proof and why unshared intuitions do not establish epistemic parity.
Demonstrate through holistic comparison that realism preserves normative judgment and deliberation with lower theoretical costs than its rivals.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish genuine causal debunking evidence from cultural variation, minority status, disagreement, or the mere absence of explicit folk metaethical views.
Require attitude-based semantics and quietism to account for counterfactual moral claims, ordinary linguistic practice, and the apparent intelligibility of metaethical questions.

routes.description: Establish global normative anti-realism by denying realism any privileged intuitive or explanatory starting point and providing pragmatist, psychological, and meaning-in-use accounts of moral judgment, language, deliberation, and opposition without objective non-naturalist facts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if realist appearances can be explained without truth-tracking access, ordinary moral practice carries no necessary realist commitment, and objective normative facts add no explanatory work beyond a more parsimonious descriptive account.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of a warranted or explanatorily necessary objective normative posit to global normative anti-realism and rejection of objective moral truths.

centralBridges.description: Show that realist intuitions and normative appearances are neither universal nor entitled to methodological priority over anti-realist starting points.
Explain moral psychology, deliberation, behavior, and discourse through attitudes, communicative intentions, social practices, and empirical causal accounts.
Establish that realism supplies no indispensable explanation and that a pragmatist framework can dissolve or bypass its proposed metaphysical problem.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify an error-producing causal history or methodological mechanism capable of explaining localized realist belief without tracking objective normative truth.
Account for sincere condemnation, counterfactual opposition, and action-guiding moral speech without committing speakers or sentences to mind-independent moral facts.

sections.title: Scope, Explananda, and Comparative Burdens
sections.rationale: The debate first turns on whether the target is morality or normativity generally, whether normative facts themselves belong among the data, and how competing theoretical packages should be compared.

sections.title: Normative Appearances and Epistemic Priority
sections.rationale: The central epistemic clash concerns whether realist appearances may function as justified starting points, whether contrary intuitions create parity, and whether disagreement without persuasion affects warrant.

sections.title: Moral Judgment, Language, and Deliberation
sections.rationale: Both routes must explain objective-seeming judgments, counterfactual wrongness, sincere condemnation, linguistic meaning, and action-guiding deliberation while establishing whether those practices carry realist commitments.

sections.title: Empirical Genealogy, Variation, and Debunking
sections.rationale: Cultural variation, folk research, minority status, shared philosophical methods, and causal error hypotheses matter insofar as they distinguish harmless diversity from a genuine debunking explanation.

sections.title: Explanatory Necessity, Parsimony, and Quietism
sections.rationale: The culminating comparative issue is whether objective normative facts perform indispensable explanatory work or whether pragmatist and descriptive accounts explain moral practice more parsimoniously and challenge the framing itself.

routes.description: Establish that Islam cannot defensibly be characterized as a religion of peace because its comprehensive and final authority claims enable coercive enforcement, its diffuse institutions cannot reliably restrain violent interpretations, and recurring intimidation or unequal rule is answered more securely by secular constitutional government.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting distinctive authority claims to material coercive consequences, showing that reformist reinterpretation lacks sufficient authority to neutralize those consequences, and explaining why observed enforcement patterns are relevant to the religion-level description rather than merely isolated misconduct.

motionBridge.description: Show that recurrent coercion grounded in Islamic claims, institutions, or enforcement practices makes peace an untenable defining description of the religion.

centralBridges.description: Connect claims of final revelation, textual perfection, submission, or comprehensive governance to intolerance of dissent and coercive enforcement.
Show that Islam's fragmented authority structure cannot authoritatively exclude violent actors or reliably displace influential rulings that legitimate violence.
Establish that censorship, sectarian violence, transnational intimidation, or political domination recur in ways materially connected to Islamic authority claims.
Explain why equal liberty and peaceful pluralism require secular constitutional institutions rather than governance grounded in asserted divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether reformist interpretations possess enough institutional force to answer explicit caliphate ambitions, punitive law, and coercive movements.
Distinguish the motion-specific evidence about Islam from general observations that other religions and political systems can also become violent.

routes.description: Establish that Islam can defensibly be characterized as a religion of peace when peace is understood as an ethical and political orientation toward justice, restraint, reconciliation, and coexistence rather than universal pacifism, while violent outcomes are traced to contested interpretations and political conditions rather than an immutable Islamic essence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by grounding a peace-oriented interpretation in Islamic concepts and traditions, demonstrating that textual and institutional plurality permits principled rejection of violence, and showing that equal citizenship, democracy, and legal restraint can be affirmed from within Islam despite extremist or authoritarian counterexamples.

motionBridge.description: Show that Islam directs human conflict toward peace, justice, and coexistence even though it acknowledges aggression and permits bounded resistance to oppression.

centralBridges.description: Ground peace, disciplined self-restraint, resistance to oppression, mutual knowledge, and respect for human diversity in an affirmative Islamic ethical account.
Establish that Islamic texts and traditions admit diverse interpretations, so violent readings do not exhaust or necessarily define the religion.
Show that Muslim scholars, councils, and inherited jurisprudential and philosophical resources can condemn violence and sustain internal reform.
Demonstrate that Muslims can affirm separated authority, common law, equal citizenship, democracy, and civic loyalty from within their religious commitments.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how dictatorship, war, historical conditions, or political instrumentalization account for prominent abuses attributed directly to Islam.
Apply a consistent standard under which abuses committed in the name of a religion or political ideal do not automatically define its normative character.

sections.title: Meaning of Peace and the Religion-Level Burden
sections.rationale: The motion depends on whether peace means pacifism, an achieved ethical orientation, or the absence of coercive institutional tendencies, and on what evidence warrants attributing a defining character to a diverse religion.

sections.title: Revelation, Religious Authority, and Interpretive Plurality
sections.rationale: The principal doctrinal clash concerns whether finality, perfection, submission, and comprehensive religious claims predict absolutism or whether plural interpretive traditions prevent any violent reading from becoming Islam's necessary meaning.

sections.title: Violence, Resistance, and Coercive Enforcement
sections.rationale: This issue tests the competing accounts of jihad and legitimate resistance alongside allegations of terrorism, sectarian violence, intimidation, blasphemy enforcement, and suppression of inquiry that bear directly on the peace predicate.

sections.title: Reform, Sharia, Secularism, and Equal Citizenship
sections.rationale: The institutional burden turns on whether Islamic law and religious citizenship can support democracy, separated authority, equal rights, and pluralism or whether only secular constitutional government can secure those goods.

sections.title: Causation, Representativeness, and Comparative Standards
sections.rationale: Religion-level conclusions require distinguishing doctrine from dictatorship, war, historical circumstance, and political manipulation while testing whether violent and peaceful examples are representative and evaluated consistently across traditions.

routes.description: Establish rationality, intentionality, content-sensitive inference, and subjective consciousness as agreed features of mind, then show that these features are more expected if mentality is fundamental than if all mental activity depends wholly on nonconscious physical processes and unguided evolution.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant mental phenomena remain insufficiently expected under naturalism after naturalistic emergence and evolutionary accounts are considered, while a mentality-fundamental hypothesis supplies a comparatively stronger explanation without requiring the argument itself to identify a uniquely theistic account.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed capacities of conscious rational minds are more probable on a non-naturalist, mentality-fundamental account than on naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that original representational aboutness is not explained merely by combining constituents that lack intentionality.
Establish that justified inference requires causation or recognition responsive to semantic and logical content, not only physical succession.
Establish that increasing behavioral or neural complexity does not by itself explain first-person subjective awareness.
Apply comparative likelihood rather than bare possibility or present explanatory incompleteness to the competing accounts.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why selection for practical success would also be expected to yield reliable abstract scientific and philosophical cognition.
Limit the conclusion to mentality or intentionality being fundamental unless further premises distinguish among non-naturalist accounts.

routes.description: Provide a naturalistic account of rational cognition through physical realization, experience, logical recognition, and selection for reliable environmental tracking, while explaining consciousness as compatible with gradual biological development and testing the comparative advantage claimed for non-naturalism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if intentional representation, inference, cognitive reliability, and consciousness can be expected through natural processes sufficiently to defeat the proposed comparative advantage, and if the observed gradual mechanisms of mental development fit naturalism at least as well as the relevant non-naturalist alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed form and development of conscious rational capacities are sufficiently expected under naturalism to defeat the claimed non-naturalist advantage.

centralBridges.description: Explain how physically constituted wholes can possess representational functions even when their individual constituents do not.
Explain why selection would favor investigative, classificatory, and inferential capacities that reliably track relevant features of the environment.
Provide a coherent path from simple responsiveness through affective awareness to abstract cognition without requiring an abrupt non-natural intervention.
Show why the observed gradual and trial-dependent mechanisms of mental development are comparatively expected under natural evolution.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for deductive trust through necessary logical relations and recognition of equivalent content across formulations.
Distinguish an incomplete naturalistic explanation from affirmative comparative support for a supernatural or otherwise non-natural cause.

sections.title: Intentionality and Physical Realization
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether original aboutness can arise in a physically constituted system and whether artifacts, emergence, or experiential representation illuminate or merely presuppose the phenomenon needing explanation.

sections.title: Inference, Deduction, and Content-Sensitive Causation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether naturalism can accommodate justified transitions between thoughts, recognition of entailment, and the role of semantic content in producing or warranting conclusions.

sections.title: Evolution and the Reliability of Reason
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether survival-oriented selection predicts generally reliable cognition, including investigative abstraction and capacities extending beyond immediate practical demands.

sections.title: Consciousness, Emergence, and Causal Role
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether gradual increases in biological complexity explain subjective awareness and whether consciousness has an adaptive, byproduct, or causally idle place within a naturalistic account.

sections.title: Comparative Likelihood and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the governing standard of comparative expectation, evaluates the evidential significance of observed developmental mechanisms, and determines how far any conclusion reaches across naturalist and non-naturalist hypotheses.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative inference from cosmic origins, physical and biological order, objective moral obligation, and immaterial features of human life to a personal creator, then explain the evidential bridge from generic theism to Christian claims.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the combined explanatory case warrants a personal, intelligent, and moral creator; survives naturalistic and anti-theist objections; and supplies a distinct evidential basis for moving from generic theism to Christianity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative evidence makes Christian theism a better account of the motion's principal domains than atheistic materialism and the anti-theist alternative.

centralBridges.description: Connect the universe's beginning and contingent existence to a supernatural personal cause while answering objections from ignorance, natural explanation, and cosmic destruction.
Connect fine-tuning and biological information to intelligent agency while addressing evolutionary explanation, underdetermination, apparent defects, suffering, and extinction.
Distinguish moral knowledge and conduct from the ontological grounding of objective obligation, then identify a transcendent moral source.
Provide an evidential route from possible divine action to resurrection and Christian authority without treating generic design or cosmic origins alone as proof of Christianity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain consciousness, rational thought, mathematics, and freedom as realities whose grounding bears on the comparison between theism and materialism.
Separate the existence question from religious wrongdoing and distinguish evidence for a creator from unsupported selection among particular deities.

routes.description: Reject the claimed inferences from unexplained or complex features of reality to a supervising deity, contest the move from a possible designer to Christianity, and establish the independent moral and political case against divine authority and organized religion.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the pro evidence does not warrant its theistic and Christian conclusions, secular accounts remain sufficient without a divine posit, and the doctrines or authority structures under review support the motion-level anti-theist critique.

motionBridge.description: Show both that God's existence has not been warranted by the offered inferences and that the proposed religious authority is morally or socially objectionable.

centralBridges.description: Maintain the claimant's burden for a creator and show why uncertainty, cosmic beginnings, order, or scientific gaps do not by themselves license a personal divine cause.
Test design and providence against natural explanation, biological underdetermination, apparent defects, extinction, suffering, and the delayed history of revelation.
Account for conscience, moral action, and self-sacrifice without divine sanction while challenging reward, punishment, and command as foundations of genuine morality.
Connect doctrines of surveillance, punishment, sacrifice, apocalypse, and claimed divine command to the anti-theist objection concerning autonomy, coercion, and political domination.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve the distinction between a speculative cosmic designer and the intervening God, miracles, resurrection, redemption, and authority claimed by Christianity.
Explain religious belief and supervision in human psychological or institutional terms without treating believers' conviction as mind-independent evidence.

sections.title: Cosmic Origins, Causation, and the Explanatory Burden
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the universe's beginning warrants a personal supernatural cause or instead leaves an unresolved question on which the theistic claimant retains the burden of proof.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Biological Information, and Providential Design
sections.rationale: This issue joins the physical and biological design inferences with objections from natural explanation, underdetermination, imperfection, suffering, extinction, and the purposes attributed to a designer.

sections.title: Objective Moral Grounding, Conscience, and Secular Virtue
sections.rationale: This issue distinguishes the grounding of objective duties from moral knowledge and behavior, while testing whether conscience, empathy, and self-sacrifice require or are altered by divine authority.

sections.title: Consciousness, Reason, Mathematics, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the cumulative argument from immaterial or normative features of human life and asks what explanatory consequences follow for theism and materialism.

sections.title: Christian Claims, Divine Authority, and the Anti-Theist Critique
sections.rationale: This issue tests the bridge from generic theism to miracles, resurrection, redemption, and Christian authority, together with objections concerning punishment, sacrifice, autonomy, coercion, and apocalyptic politics.

routes.description: Establish that objective moral values require a transcendent standard of goodness and that objective duties require authoritative imperatives, then show that a necessarily good divine nature and commands grounded in that nature provide those foundations while naturalism does not.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects objective value to God's necessarily good nature, objective duty to competent divine authority, and the inadequacy of evolutionary, cultural, preference-based, or well-being facts to supply equivalent objective and binding foundations.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties have a supernatural rather than wholly natural ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Explain how God's necessarily good nature constitutes a nonarbitrary standard of objective moral value.
Explain how commands issued by competent divine authority and constrained by divine goodness constitute objective moral duties.
Show why natural facts about evolution, consciousness, preference, suffering, or flourishing do not alone establish objective moral value or binding obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the existence and ground of moral facts from moral language, moral knowledge, and disagreement about their application.
Account for the agency and responsibility presupposed by objective duties and address whether naturalistic determinism can sustain them.

routes.description: Establish that value arises through conscious experience, that facts about suffering and flourishing permit objective comparison and correction, and that rational scientific inquiry can investigate those facts, while showing that divine nature, commands, or revelation are unnecessary or unsuitable foundations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it derives an objective natural standard from conscious well-being, explains how inquiry can distinguish better and worse states independently of current opinion, and shows that supernatural authority neither supplies a necessary standard nor resolves arbitrariness and harmful-command objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties can be founded in natural facts about conscious creatures without supernatural authority.

centralBridges.description: Establish conscious experience as the domain in which suffering, flourishing, and morally relevant value can exist.
Explain how movement away from extreme misery toward flourishing supports objective comparisons and allows preferences, practices, and judgments to be mistaken.
Show how objective reasoning and scientific inquiry can investigate natural facts governing conscious well-being despite foundational axioms and first-person experience.
Show why defining divine nature as good or grounding duties in commands does not independently establish goodness and can conflict with judgments about suffering and harm.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend well-being as a usable objective standard despite incomplete definitions, plural forms of flourishing, and difficult boundary cases.
Address whether competing revelations, inherited traditions, and disputed purported commands provide reliable access to moral truth.

sections.title: The Ontological Ground of Objective Moral Value
sections.rationale: This issue tests the primary competing foundations: necessarily good divine nature on the supernatural route and conscious experience, suffering, and flourishing on the natural route.

sections.title: Well-Being, Moral Objectivity, and Scientific Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether natural facts permit objective comparisons, correction of preferences and cultures, and rational investigation despite axioms, subjective experience, or imprecise boundaries.

sections.title: From Facts to Objective Duties and Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue addresses how either route moves from descriptions or values to binding obligations, including authority, the fact-value distinction, agency, ability, and responsibility.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Command, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether divine nature constrains commands nonarbitrarily and whether commands involving apparent harm can be assessed by a standard independent of their asserted source.

sections.title: Moral Ontology, Knowledge, Disagreement, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue distinguishes moral reality from access to it and tests the significance of disagreement, competing religious traditions, inherited belief, and shared inquiry for each foundational route.

routes.description: Establish that multiple independent features of reality—including cosmic origins, life-permitting conditions, moral objectivity, the historical case concerning Jesus, and immediate experience—provide convergent support for a transcendent personal God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one major inference, or the cumulative interaction of several inferences, supplies a warranted bridge from the available evidence to supernatural personal agency while relevant naturalistic alternatives and epistemic objections are addressed.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative philosophical, scientific, moral, historical, and experiential evidence to the conclusion that God's existence is supported.

centralBridges.description: Show that the universe's beginning or life-permitting structure warrants an inference to transcendent personal causation or design.
Show that objective moral values and duties are real and require a foundation beyond naturalistic processes or collective human practice.
Show that the historical claims concerning Jesus are sufficiently grounded and are best accounted for by divine action.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify the deductive, explanatory, or cumulative form of the theistic inferences and the burden applicable to their premises.
Establish when immediate moral or religious experience may provide warranted belief absent a sufficient defeater.

routes.description: Establish philosophical naturalism as the warranted position by affirming the known natural world and showing that the proposed cosmological, design, moral, historical, and experiential bridges to supernatural reality lack sufficient justification.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available evidence does not warrant any proposed bridge from nature to God and continued natural explanation or withholding supernatural belief remains justified without requiring proof that every supernatural possibility is impossible.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available evidence does not provide a sufficiently justified bridge from known nature to God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Defend evidential restraint toward untestable supernatural claims while explaining why belief in known nature may be retained.
Preserve live natural explanations or relevant uncertainty for cosmic origins and life-permitting conditions.
Explain how objective but nonabsolute morality can arise through human experience, comparison, deliberation, and social practice.
Show that historical testimony, miracle reports, and conflicting religious experiences do not uniquely establish supernatural causation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify why withholding supernatural belief can be compatible with either atheistic or agnostic terminology.
Determine whether adaptable theological explanations discriminate among favorable, unfavorable, and religiously conflicting observations.

sections.title: Epistemic Burdens, Inference Form, and Naturalism
sections.rationale: This issue governs what counts as an evidential bridge beyond nature, whether theistic arguments are deductive or explanatory, and whether failed supernatural inferences warrant naturalism, atheism, agnosticism, or suspended judgment.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning and Transcendent Causation
sections.rationale: The universe's temporal or causal origin supplies a direct proposed route beyond physical reality, while questions about infinity, timeless personhood, and further natural reality test whether that route reaches God.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Life, and Design
sections.rationale: The evidential significance of life-permitting constants depends on necessity, chance, probability spaces, possible forms of life, broader cosmic populations, and whether design provides a discriminating explanation.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Knowledge, and Grounding
sections.rationale: Moral experience and objective obligation form a principal proposed inference to God, while distinctions among ontology, knowledge, absoluteness, intersubjective practice, evolution, and moral progress define the central clash.

sections.title: Resurrection, Historical Sources, and Miracle Claims
sections.rationale: The specifically Christian route turns on the historical use of New Testament materials, corroboration standards, natural alternatives, testimony, and whether resurrection or miracle claims warrant an inference to divine action.

sections.title: Religious Experience and Conflicting Revelations
sections.rationale: Immediate experience is offered as direct warrant for God, while incompatible religious reports and the need for a method of corroboration bear on whether such experience identifies supernatural truth.

routes.description: Establish classical theism through convergent arguments from contingent existence, change and causal finitude, then identify the necessary ground as personal, knowledgeable, powerful, and good while defending this conclusion against objections from quantum randomness, freedom, and suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if contingent and changing reality requires a necessary explanatory cause, the cause has attributes sufficient for the motion-level identification with God, moral facts reinforce divine goodness, and evil and quantum indeterminacy do not defeat those inferences.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary explanatory cause and its derived personal, cognitive, powerful, and good attributes to the conclusion that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Show that contingent reality, change, and any finite causal history require an uncaused, purely actual, necessarily existing explanatory ground.
Derive timelessness, immateriality, power, personality, and knowledge from the nature and explanatory role of the first cause.
Show that objective moral facts, human worth, and responsibility require or support a perfectly good divine foundation.
Show that suffering can be permitted for greater goods or prevention of greater evils and therefore does not contradict or outweigh the case for God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend an existence-focused principle of sufficient reason that remains applicable even if particular quantum outcomes are probabilistic.
Defend agent causation and irreducible intentionality as support for free responsibility and personal explanation.

routes.description: Withhold theistic belief by challenging the premises and divine identification of the affirmative causal case, disputing its moral and free-will commitments, and presenting apparently gratuitous animal suffering as evidence that fits a loving, perfectly good God less well than a non-theistic world.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if sufficient reason and the first-cause inferences remain unsupported or internally costly, moral considerations do not establish God, and the quantity or character of suffering supplies an unresolved evidential reason against the proposed divine attributes.

motionBridge.description: Connect the underdetermination of the affirmative arguments and the evidence from apparently gratuitous suffering to agnostic nonacceptance of theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that sufficient reason risks assuming an ultimate terminus, conflicts with quantum indeterminacy, or permits an unexplained cosmic event when narrowed.
Show that causal or explanatory reasoning does not adequately establish a personal divine agent rather than another ultimate foundation.
Challenge objective ought-claims, divine moral grounding, and the compatibility of sufficient explanation with libertarian responsibility.
Show that apparently unnecessary animal suffering and the possibility of less evil are improbable under a loving and perfectly good creator.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use freedom without earthly suffering in heaven to test whether grave evil is necessary for free agency, virtue, or perfected relationship.
Require independent truth-directed support beyond internal coherence and resist appeals to inaccessible divine reasons that presuppose the disputed deity.

sections.title: Contingency, Change, and the Necessary Ground
sections.rationale: This issue contains the foundational affirmative inferences from contingent existence, actualization, and causal finitude, together with the objection that sufficient explanation assumes rather than establishes an ultimate terminus.

sections.title: Sufficient Reason and Quantum Randomness
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether quantum indeterminacy defeats the explanatory principle, whether probabilistic causes remain sufficient, and whether narrowing the principle preserves or undercuts the inference from the universe to a necessary being.

sections.title: Divine Attributes and Personal Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue governs the indispensable transition from a generic cause or necessary foundation to a timeless, immaterial, powerful, knowledgeable, and personal being recognizable as God.

sections.title: Morality, Freedom, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether objective value, human worth, obligation, and responsibility support divine grounding, as well as whether metaethical skepticism or explanatory determinism blocks that route.

sections.title: Evil, Animal Suffering, and Greater-Good Defenses
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal affirmative evidence against a loving and perfectly good God and the principal theistic replies involving greater goods, regular natural order, worthwhile existence, human epistemic limits, and heavenly freedom.
